steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on coverage path planning with space-filling curves where the robot avoids obstacles online. Give background on SFCs and their uses, review SFC-based robotic exploration and where it falls short with obstacles, then state our contributions and how the paper is organized.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Origins and properties of space-filling curves
2. Applications of SFCs
3. Robotic exploration and the coverage planning problem
4. Why SFCs suit exploration
5. Prior SFC-based exploration work and its limits with obstacles
6. Gap, contributions and paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Origins and properties of SFCs
- 1878: George Cantor, interval I=[0, 1] mapped bijectively onto [0, 1]\times[0, 1]
- G. Peano: such a mapping that is also continuous and surjective; image when parameterized in I to higher dimensions (\mathbb{R}^{n}) = Space-Filling Curve (SFC)
- more SFCs: E. Moore, H. Lebesgue, W. Sierpinski, G. Polya
- self-similar: sub-curves similar to whole curve
- surjective: cover every point in \mathbb{R}^{n}
- locality preserving: close in I -> close in \mathbb{R}^{n}

2. Applications
- data collection from sensor networks
- ordering meshes of complex geometries
- approximate TSP solution via Hilbert's curve
- Space Filling Trees (tree-like analogue) for sampling-based path planning, vs. RRTs

3. Robotic exploration / CPP
- single or group of robots search, survey, gather info about a region while avoiding obstacles
- sub-problem of Coverage Planning Problem (CPP): visit all points in a 2D area or volume
- CPP approaches: graph based, grid based, neural-network based, cellular decomposition based
- each usable for exploration

4. Why SFCs for exploration
- time complete, robust to failure
- Hilbert's curve more efficient in time of travel / cost of task than lawnmower's path
- 2D strategies extend to 3D (similar construction grammar)
- Generalized SFC (GSFC): irregular quadrilaterals and triangles
- easy to use for non-uniform coverage

5. Prior work
- swarm of mobile robots, each following an SFC: energy efficient, robust, finite-time coverage; obstacle-free
- non-uniform coverage planning for UAVs; extended with Hilbert curve, optimal vs. non-SFC methods
- UAV aerial localization system using Moore's SFC
- these three: no obstacles
- path planning for SFCs with obstacles, optimal for specific obstacle configurations (Hamiltonian path)
- SFCs for sensor networks with holes -> motion planning with obstacles
- both need obstacle knowledge before exploration
- online evasion for Hilbert curve, one waypoint blocked
- follow-up: two neighboring waypoints on Hilbert curve
- online avoidance for aerial vehicle with Sierpinski curve; obstacles must block disjoint cells

6. Gap, contributions, organization
- early work: no obstacles; later: prior knowledge needed or restricted obstacle class / SFC
- next step: online strategy, arbitrary obstacles, any SFC
- contribution: online, uses grid connectivity of SFC cells
- contribution: any SFC, any number of randomly placed obstacles
- contribution: non-uniform coverage
- five sections: II SFCs; III problem + strategy; IV properties + examples; V conclusion, limitations, future work

steps.text:
In 1878 George Cantor showed that the interval I=[0, 1] can be mapped bijectively onto the square [0, 1]\times[0, 1]. After that G. Peano found a mapping like this which is also continuous and surjective. When such a mapping is parameterized in the interval I to higher dimensions (\mathbb{R}^{n}), its image is called a Space-Filling Curve (SFC). Later more SFCs were discovered by E. Moore, H. Lebesgue, W. Sierpinski and G. Polya. SFCs have some interesting properties. First they are self-similar, which means every curve is made of sub-curves that are similar to the whole curve. They are also surjective maps, so they cover every point in \mathbb{R}^{n}. And they preserve locality, so points that are close in I are also close in \mathbb{R}^{n}.

Because of these properties SFCs are used in a lot of applications, for example data collection from sensor networks and ordering meshes of complex geometries. Hilbert's Space Filling curve can be used to find an approximate solution to the Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP). Also Space Filling Trees, which are analogous to SFCs but have a tree-like structure, have been proposed for sampling-based path planning instead of traditional methods like Rapid-exploring Random Trees (RRTs).

In the robotic exploration problem, one robotic agent or a group of them is deployed to search, survey or gather information about a specific region and they have to avoid obstacles while doing it. Robotic exploration is a sub-problem of the bigger Coverage Planning Problem (CPP), where the agent has the task of visiting all points in a 2D area or a volume. There are already many approaches for CPP, such as graph based, grid based, neural-network based and cellular decomposition based approaches. Each of them can be used for the robotic exploration problem.

SFCs have also been used for robotic exploration because of the useful properties they have. Exploration with SFCs is time complete and it is robust to failure. It has been shown that Hilbert's curve is more efficient in time of travel / cost of task than the lawnmower's path. Strategies for exploration developed in 2D using SFCs can be extended to 3D, because a similar grammar exists for constructing them in both dimensions. The generalized version, Generalized SFC (GSFC), can span irregular quadrilaterals and triangles. SFCs can also easily be used for non-uniform coverage, where some parts need to be searched more rigorously than other parts.

- UAV aerial localization system using Moore's SFC

- follow-up: two neighboring waypoints on Hilbert curve

- next step: online strategy, arbitrary obstacles, any SFC
- contribution: online, uses grid connectivity of SFC cells

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In 1878 George Cantor showed that the interval I=[0, 1] can be mapped bijectively onto the square [0, 1]\times[0, 1]. After that G. Peano found a mapping like this which is also continuous and surjective. When such a mapping is parameterized in the interval I to higher dimensions (\mathbb{R}^{n}), its image is called a Space-Filling Curve (SFC). Later more SFCs were discovered by E. Moore, H. Lebesgue, W. Sierpinski and G. Polya. SFCs have some interesting properties. First they are self-similar, which means every curve is made of sub-curves that are similar to the whole curve. They are also surjective maps, so they cover every point in \mathbb{R}^{n}. And they preserve locality, so points that are close in I are also close in \mathbb{R}^{n}.

Because of these properties SFCs are used in a lot of applications, for example data collection from sensor networks and ordering meshes of complex geometries. Hilbert's Space Filling curve can be used to find an approximate solution to the Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP). Also Space Filling Trees, which are analogous to SFCs but have a tree-like structure, have been proposed for sampling-based path planning instead of traditional methods like Rapid-exploring Random Trees (RRTs).

In the robotic exploration problem, one robotic agent or a group of them is deployed to search, survey or gather information about a specific region and they have to avoid obstacles while doing it. Robotic exploration is a sub-problem of the bigger Coverage Planning Problem (CPP), where the agent has the task of visiting all points in a 2D area or a volume. There are already many approaches for CPP, such as graph based, grid based, neural-network based and cellular decomposition based approaches. Each of them can be used for the robotic exploration problem.

SFCs have also been used for robotic exploration because of the useful properties they have. Exploration with SFCs is time complete and it is robust to failure. It has been shown that Hilbert's curve is more efficient in time of travel / cost of task than the lawnmower's path. Strategies for exploration developed in 2D using SFCs can be extended to 3D, because a similar grammar exists for constructing them in both dimensions. The generalized version, Generalized SFC (GSFC), can span irregular quadrilaterals and triangles. SFCs can also easily be used for non-uniform coverage, where some parts need to be searched more rigorously than other parts.

There is a sizable literature on SFC based robotic exploration. One work suggests using a swarm of mobile robots for exploration where each robot follows an SFC. This approach is energy efficient, robust to failures and makes sure coverage happens in finite time, but the environment is assumed to be obstacle-free. Another work proposes a new method for non-uniform coverage planning for UAVs. A later work takes this further and uses the Hilbert curve for non-uniform coverage, which is optimal compared to existing methods that do not use SFC. A UAV system for aerial localization that uses Moore's SFC has also been introduced. But none of these three works considers obstacles.

One approach for path planning with SFCs and obstacles was introduced and its optimality was proved for specific obstacle configurations, because a Hamiltonian path exists for those configurations. Another work introduced an algorithm to construct SFCs for sensor networks that have holes, and this algorithm can be used for motion planning with obstacles using SFC. But both of these solutions need to know about the obstacles before the exploration starts.

An online obstacle evasion strategy was formulated for the Hilbert curve but only for the case where one waypoint is blocked by an obstacle. Another strategy builds on the path planning approach above and can evade two neighboring waypoints on a Hilbert curve. There is also work on online obstacle avoidance for an aerial vehicle covering a region using the Sierpinski curve, but there the obstacles have to block disjoint cells.

So early work did not consider obstacles in the environment. Later works did consider obstacles, but they needed knowledge about the obstacles or they were restricted to a particular class of obstacles and SFC. So the next step that is needed is an online strategy that can go around arbitrary obstacles while using any SFC, and this is what our proposed strategy does. The contributions of the paper are:

- The proposed strategy is online and avoids obstacles on the go by using the grid connectivity of the SFC cells.
- The strategy works for any SFC and any number of obstacles placed randomly in the environment.
- The strategy can be used for non-uniform coverage.

The rest of the paper has five sections. Section II introduces SFCs formally. Section III formulates the problem and presents the proposed strategy. Section IV discusses the properties of the strategy and the examples we implemented. Section V concludes the paper and discusses limitations and possible future work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In 1878, George Cantor demonstrated that an interval I=[0,1] can be mapped bijectively onto [0,1]\times[0,1]. Later, G. Peano discovered one such mapping that is also continuous and surjective; the image of such a mapping, when parameterized in the interval I to higher dimensions (\mathbb{R}^{n}), is known as a Space-Filling Curve (SFC). More SFCs were later discovered by E. Moore, H. Lebesgue, W. Sierpinski, and G. Polya [1,2]. SFCs have several interesting properties. They are self-similar, meaning each curve consists of sub-curves similar to the entire curve. They are also surjective maps, so they cover every point in \mathbb{R}^{n}. Finally, they preserve locality: points close in I remain close in \mathbb{R}^{n}.

Due to these properties, SFCs have been used in many applications, such as data collection from sensor networks [3,4] and ordering meshes of complex geometries [2]. An approximate solution to the Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) can be found using Hilbert's Space Filling curve [5]. Space Filling Trees, analogous to SFCs but with a tree-like structure, have been proposed for sampling-based path planning [6], as opposed to traditional methods like Rapid-exploring Random Trees (RRTs) [7].

In the robotic exploration problem, a single robotic agent or a group of them is deployed to search, survey or gather information about a specific region while avoiding obstacles. Robotic exploration is one of the sub-problems of the larger Coverage Planning Problem (CPP), in which the agent is given the task of visiting all points in a 2D area or volume [8,9,10,11]. Numerous approaches for CPP already exist - Graph based, Grid based, Neural-Network based and Cellular decomposition based [8] - and each of them can be used for the robotic exploration problem.

SFCs have been utilized for robotic exploration because of the advantageous properties they possess. Exploration using SFCs is time complete and robust to failure [12]. Hilbert's curve has been shown to be more efficient in time of travel / cost of task than the lawnmower's path [13]. Exploration strategies developed for 2D using SFCs can be extended to 3D, since a similar grammar exists for their construction in both dimensions [2]. The generalized version of SFCs, Generalized SFC (GSFC), can span irregular quadrilaterals and triangles [2]. SFCs can also easily be used in non-uniform coverage scenarios, where some parts must be searched more rigorously than others.

There is a sizable literature on SFC based robotic exploration. [12] suggests using a swarm of mobile robots for exploration, with each robot following an SFC. This approach is energy efficient, robust to failures and assures coverage in finite time, but it considers an obstacle-free environment. [14] proposes a novel method for non-uniform coverage planning for UAVs. [13] takes this work further and uses the Hilbert curve for non-uniform coverage, which is optimal compared with existing methods not using SFC. [15] introduced a UAV system for aerial localization that uses Moore's SFC. However, [14,13,15] do not consider obstacles.

[16] introduced a path planning approach for SFCs with obstacles and proved its optimality for specific obstacle configurations, owing to the existence of a Hamiltonian path for such configurations. [17] introduced an algorithm to construct SFCs for sensor networks with holes, which can be used for motion planning with obstacles using SFC. However, the solutions in [16,17] require knowledge of the obstacles before exploration starts.

[18] formulated an online obstacle evasion strategy for the Hilbert curve when only one waypoint is blocked by an obstacle. [19] builds upon [16] and suggests a strategy that can evade two neighboring waypoints on a Hilbert curve. [20] discusses online obstacle avoidance for an aerial vehicle covering a region using the Sierpinski curve, but the obstacles need to block disjoint cells.

Early work on the topic did not consider obstacles in the environment. Later works considered obstacles but required knowledge about them or were restricted to a particular class of obstacles and SFC. Hence, the necessary next step is an online strategy that can navigate around arbitrary obstacles while employing any SFC, which is what the proposed strategy addresses. The contributions of the paper are:

- The proposed strategy is online and avoids obstacles on the go using the grid connectivity of the SFC cells.
- The strategy is applicable to any SFC and any number of obstacles placed randomly in the environment.
- The strategy can be used for non-uniform coverage.

The rest of this paper is organized into five sections: Section II formally introduces SFCs. Section III formulates the problem and presents the proposed strategy. Section IV discusses the properties of the strategy and the implemented examples. Section V concludes the paper and discusses limitations and possible future work.

[2] Bader, M., 2012. Space-filling curves: an introduction with applications in scientific computing (Vol. 9). Springer Science & Business Media.
